Well if it's a detective story with a Sam Spade/Humphrey Bogart type lead, a dead body and a missing fortune are pretty much prerequisites.


But there are noirs about fixed boxing matches like *The Set-Up*, that aren't explicitly about a murder, but they're few and far between.
[removed]

Well, The Big Lebowski is stoner neo noir, with The Dude as Sam Spade if instead of a private dick he was a stoned, unemployed slacker. Someone dies in the film, but it’s not a murder, and the main mystery is about a kidnapping.

Sweet Smell of Success is an incredibly dark film from that time that I don’t think has any death in it. There is violence, but no murder.

Rififi is a classic French heist flick that does not centre around murder.

The Wages of Fear is about four men driving dangerous nitroglycerin through South America on treacherous roads. It’s not strictly a noir film by some definitions, but it shares a nihilism and cynicism with a lot of noir films from that era.

One thing I would say though is that noir is typically a genre/style that was about uncovering the dark underbelly of post-war America, and naturally that usually involves violence and murder. A central theme involves the threat to the idyllic modern American lifestyle, where characters are desperate and therefore do desperate things.

There are a number of noirs where murder is not at the centre of the story, or where the murder of someone happens more as a catalyst for the story, like The Maltese Falcon and Key Largo.

Lastly, Out of the Past has murder in it, but I would say is one of the more romantic (in a fatalistic way) films from the classic period.
I'll check out the set-up, thank you!

the wages of fear sounds particularly interesting. I was thinking maybe political thriller type films might be a good place to look.
I’d highly recommend all of them, and Wages of Fear is great regardless of whether it strictly fits the “noir” category or not.

I consider Bicycle Thieves to be more of a drama than a noir, but because the subject matter is so difficult, I'm mentioning it.

Also Citizen Kane as far as I remember doesn't have an intentional murder, and I consider that film to be kind of the prototyping of early noir techniques.

Now Singing in the Rain definitely isn't a Noir, but had a burlesque scene with Cyd Charise in which Gene Kelly tries his best at being this hard boiled Sam Spade like character.

I think it's a great example of showing how the arguable elements of bleak black and white storytelling with Hays code limitations or something that takes on a different atmosphere with glamorous color and in your face sexiness.

And to cap things off..

I don't think 'to have and  have not' is exactly noir ( I considered to be a wartime Thriller) but it does kind of have that cigarettes and nightclub vibe that is known for being kind of a Trope of the genre.

So I think Citizen Kane is your best bet for a film immersed with the type of bleak intensity that would be associated with the nor film surrounding it.

Hope this helps!

Is the aim to find something unconventional?  Because I have something completely out of left field:

 American Beauty (1998) by Sam Mendes

[Opening Scene](https://youtu.be/XMqwSTe5rvo?si=nOgmtpjFWwtnf-my)

Interesting! I just watched the opening scene and I can see how it fits u/buffaluffasaurus' def of noir being about exposing the underbelly of post-war American suburbia. 

Yes, I think that's exactly it (wanting unconventional noir) I guess I got started thinking about what makes noir, noir and watching to watch more genre-pushing noir. (For example Dementia has no dialogue or VO, but the cinematography and plot is very noir.)
The Set-Up is such a great little film.
[removed]

Yes, American Beauty definitely deals with post-war American suburbia more directly within the film.  

The VO, the beginning starting with the end, among a few other things, don't just resemble noir; they're straight of the noir playbook.  There's even a blonde femme fatale.

I had seen the movie a few times but after one of my film classes started talking about the noir structure and themes, it just clicked into place, and quite perfectly.

Many people see it as a straight suburban existential angst dramedy film, but through the lens of noir, it takes on a whole new meaning.

Decision to Leave might not be a noir per se, but might tick the box for you. I’d say more crime thriller/ drama. Lots of turns and mysteries. I don’t want to give too much away if you haven’t seen it, but I’d say it’s similar to Brick in the sense a murder happens and sets off the character’s journeys. There is a little murder, which sounds like it might be a no go. However, it’s not the focus of the film. 
The film came out in 2022 so it should be easy to find on streaming.
